chapters.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Herzog, despite branding himself an anti-intellectual who dismisses critics with 'Go for it, losers!' and lives 'with as little reflection as possible,' has a genuine philosophy of filmmaking centered on 'ecstatic truth' against the 'accountant's truth.' It reads his persona of 'false Herzogs' and doppelgangers as itself a rhetorical construction, and invokes Wittgenstein's 'Don't think, but look!' to frame Herzog's demand that viewers approach films like Grizzly Man and Fitzcarraldo with open eyes rather than academic categories. It surveys each contributor's essay as a way of restoring the 'effability' of Herzog's work.

chapters.file: ch07 - “I Am What My Films Are”.md
chapters.relation: David LaRocca listens to Herzog's essayistic, self-mythologizing pronouncements in autobiographical documentaries like 'I Am My Films' and 'Werner Herzog: Filmemacher,' arguing that Herzog practices a 'vigorous essayism' that yields 'ecstatic truth' from fabrication (as in the story of walking to Paris to save Lotte Eisner, or seeing God who turned out to be a power-station worker). Drawing on Deleuze's remark on the defenseless walker and a Nietzschean stress on what is 'healthiest,' LaRocca connects Herzog's virtue of filmmaking-on-foot and his Rogue Film School anti-pedagogy to a 'humanistic sublime' that returns us to human limits and mortality rather than transcending them.

chapters.file: ch08 - Herzog’s Sublime and Ecstatic Truth.md
chapters.relation: Patricia Castello Branco argues that Herzog's sublime is Burkean and physiological rather than Kantian and transcendental: in Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo, and Grizzly Man the protagonists' encounter with overwhelming nature defeats reason and works through the body (Kinski's distorted performance, Treadwell's death) rather than confirming reason's supremacy as in Kant's Critique of Judgment. She maps Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' onto Nietzsche's Dionysian from The Birth of Tragedy, where the principium individuationis dissolves and the hero merges with nature's creating-and-destroying flux, and glosses ecstatic truth via Heidegger's aletheia as unconcealment reached through fabrication and stylization.

chapters.file: ch09 - The Conquest of Uselessness as a Practice of Film and Thought.md
chapters.relation: Daniele Dottorini reads Herzog's filmmaking as a 'conquest of the useless' through the figures of the Tightrope Walker (Philippe Petit), the Traveler, and the Pilgrim, whose bodily effort and risk over the abyss subtract film from any utilitarian logic. He aligns them with the tightrope walker of the prologue to Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, poised between animal and Overman, and uses Deleuze and Guattari's 'conceptual personae' from What Is Philosophy? to argue that Herzog becomes his own characters. The carrying of the ship over the mountain in Fitzcarraldo and Steiner's ecstatic ski-flight exemplify ecstatic truth (aletheia) as an unveiling that transfigures the world into music.

chapters.file: ch10 - Filmmaking and Philosophizing against the Grain of Theory Herzog and Wittgenstein.md
chapters.relation: Mihai Ometita pairs Herzog's anti-intellectualism with Wittgenstein's later philosophy, arguing that the obstinacy of Herzog's protagonists (Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo) and the dogmatism of Wittgenstein's interlocutors are two faces of an unbounded attachment to a single theory. Herzog's dictum 'An ape is an ape' echoes Wittgenstein's motto that everything is what it is, warning against forced metaphor (the smoking monkey in Echoes from a Somber Empire). Citing the Big Typescript and On Certainty, Ometita reads philosophy's difficulty as one of the will, and treats Aguirre's 'delirium' and Fitzcarraldo's 'dream' as quasi-nonsense that resists hasty diagnoses of madness; he invokes Descartes's window and Merleau-Ponty on film being perceived, not thought.

chapters.file: ch11 - Nature and Natural Meaning in Grizzly Man.md
chapters.relation: Marc Furstenau reads Grizzly Man as Herzog's philosophy of nature, arguing that Herzog's vision of nature as chaos, hostility, and murder mirrors Schopenhauer's terrifying Will and the fact/value split, and that Herzog blames Timothy Treadwell's sentimental faith in natural harmony for his and Amie Huguenard's deaths while secretly sharing Treadwell's amor fati. Using Iris Murdoch's Metaphysics as a Guide to Morals and Mary Midgley's Beast and Man, Furstenau contends that both Herzog and Schopenhauer succumb to an 'outrageous simplicity' that denies animal agency; against them he argues, via Midgley, that culture is natural and interspecies sympathy is real, reading Treadwell's extreme close-up of the bear (where Herzog sees 'only the overwhelming indifference of nature') as evidence of imaginative continuity between human and animal.

chapters.file: ch12 - Reflections from the Abyss Herzog’s Philosophy of Death.md
chapters.relation: M. Blake Wilson traces Herzog's philosophy of death and the 'abyss' across Grizzly Man and Into the Abyss, examining how Herzog frames human, animal, and self-killings and refuses the retributive impulse. Against Kant's demand that murderers must die and Matthew Kramer's purgative rationale for capital punishment, Wilson enlists Nietzsche's warnings about the drive to punish and Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us,' while contrasting Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' with the 'accountant's truth' via journalistic and bear-attack literature (Jans, Herrero) that accuses Herzog of a 'Hollywoodized' portrait of Treadwell. He coins 'vivicide' for the killing of a human by a non-human animal and questions whether Bear 141 committed murder or was merely a scavenger.

chapters.file: ch13 - Fake News and Ecstatic Truths.md
chapters.relation: Kyle Novak uses Herzog's fabricated Pascal epigraph in Lessons of Darkness to distinguish 'ecstatic truth' from Trump-era 'alternative facts,' arguing that unlike Kellyanne Conway's deception, Herzog openly reveals his inventions to deepen an artistic experience. Rejecting Russell's correspondence theory of truth, Novak turns to Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation and The Gulf War Did Not Take Place to show how media create norms and a hyperreality independent of facts, then to Nietzsche's 'On Truth and Lies' (truth as agreed-upon metaphor) and Deleuze's affirmation of life as a non-relativist standard, concluding that Lessons of Darkness is 'sparse on facts but full of truths' that penetrate deeper than CNN footage.
